Opportunity Modeling: WR Targets

Research question: How predictive are raw targets of fantasy WR success, and how does predictive power compare against Target Share? This is a research module for future Opportunity Model components, not a breakout study and not a ranking system.

Fantasy Production by Opportunity

Average half-PPR points per game across increasing opportunity buckets
PPG
The 150+ targets bucket posts the strongest average output at 15.2 PPG (n=62). Largest jump: <50 to 50-75 (+3.9 PPG).

Starter Probability Curve

Chance of finishing as a Top 24 fantasy wide receiver
Top 24
WRs in the 150+ targets bucket historically reach Top 24 rate 95.2% of the time (n=62). Largest jump: 100-125 to 125-150 (+43.5 pts).

WR1 Probability Curve

Chance of finishing inside the season-long Top 12
Top 12
WRs in the 150+ targets bucket historically reach Top 12 probability 87.1% of the time (n=62). Largest jump: 125-150 to 150+ (+45.6 pts).

Elite Outcome Curve

Chance of reaching a Top 5 positional finish
Top 5
WRs in the 150+ targets bucket historically reach Top 5 probability 56.5% of the time (n=62). Largest jump: 125-150 to 150+ (+43.7 pts).

League Winner Probability

Chance of finishing as the overall WR1
WR1
WRs in the 150+ targets bucket historically reach WR1 overall rate 12.9% of the time (n=62). Largest jump: 125-150 to 150+ (+10.8 pts).

Conclusion

  • Targets are strongly directional for WR fantasy success, especially once raw volume moves into the 100+ and 125+ target buckets.
  • Compared with Target Share, this study's standalone comparison favors Target Share across correlation and elite-outcome separation.
  • Targets should be included as a future WR Opportunity Score component, but paired with Target Share so the model captures both absolute volume and team-context-adjusted opportunity.
